claims.text: A minor amount of zirconia or titania can enhance the thermal stability of multielement solid-solution nanoparticles at 773–1173 K.
The refractory metal oxide will form a stabilizing shell around the nanoparticles.
The refractory metal oxide may decorate the nanoparticle surface.
An oxide shell or surface decoration will reduce surface diffusion.
Reduced surface diffusion will prevent particle coarsening.
The oxide dopant will reduce nanoparticle surface energy.
Reduced surface energy will lower the driving force for Ostwald ripening and coarsening.
Suppressing Ostwald ripening and coarsening will enhance nanoparticle thermal stability.
Doped nanoparticles will undergo less particle coarsening than untreated nanoparticles.
Doped nanoparticles will retain better catalytic performance than untreated nanoparticles.
Untreated nanoparticles will undergo significant coarsening during operation at 773–1173 K.
Untreated nanoparticles will suffer degradation in catalytic performance during operation at 773–1173 K.
The intervention is expected to work for nanoparticles containing at least five metals and less than 50% total noble-metal content.
The intervention is expected to work throughout the operating range of 773–1173 K.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes the oxide as a dopant introduced into the multielement nanoparticles, whereas the structural mediator places it in a shell or as surface decoration. Bulk incorporation and a separate surface phase are materially distinct interventions, and the intended configuration is unresolved.
